name: Bhaktavatsala Perumal Temple, Thiruninravur
deity: Vishnu as Bhaktavatsala Perumal, standing and facing east, with the Goddess Ennai Petra Thayar (Sudhavalli)
period: A Divya Desam of Thondai Nadu, honoured by Thirumangai Alvar in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham
dynasty: Pallava origins, with later Chola and Vijayanagara additions
summary: On the western edge of Chennai, Vishnu stands as Bhaktavatsala Perumal, the lord who loves his devotees — a Divya Desam of Thondai Nadu, also remembered as Srinivasa Kshetram.

sections.history: Thiruninravur, on the western outskirts of Chennai, is one of the 108 Divya Desams in Thondai Nadu, praised by Thirumangai Alvar in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham. The temple is believed to have been raised by the Pallavas in the late eighth century, with later contributions from the medieval Cholas and the Vijayanagara kings. The place is also called Srinivasa Kshetram, as Vishnu is said to have made his abode here. Tradition tells that Thirumangai Alvar passed through without singing a full decad, and that the Lord followed him; his two verses on this Lord are found within decads sung at other shrines. The temple is today administered by the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments department.
sections.architecture: The temple is entered beneath a gateway tower of the Vijayanagara period, and gathers around the sanctum of Bhaktavatsala Perumal, who stands facing east. The Goddess Ennai Petra Thayar, also called Sudhavalli, has her own shrine. Its sacred tank is the Varuna Pushkarini, for Varuna is said to have worshipped Vishnu here. Daily worship follows six rituals through the day. In the same town stands the Hridayaleeswarar temple of Shiva, linked with the Nayanar Poosalar, who built a temple to the Lord in his heart.
sections.legends: The sthala purana tells that Lakshmi came to this place, and her father Samudra Raja, the lord of the ocean, followed her and addressed her as Ennai Petra Thayar — the mother who bore me. From this the Goddess takes her name here. Tradition also says that Vishnu stayed at this kshetra, hence its other name, Srinivasa Kshetram, and that when Thirumangai Alvar went by without singing, the Lord came after him. Versions of the tale differ in detail, but all return to the lord's love for his devotees.
sections.festivals: Vaikunta Ekadashi is the greatest day of the year, when devotees gather before dawn for the opening of the northern gateway. The yearly Brahmotsavam brings the processional deity out through the streets of the town on a succession of vahanas. Confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Thiruninravur is among the easiest Divya Desams to reach from Chennai, yet it keeps a village-temple calm. Visitors first see the Vijayanagara-period gateway, then stand before Bhaktavatsala Perumal. Many make a point of offering respects at the shrine of Ennai Petra Thayar, whose name carries the whole tenderness of the tale. The Varuna Pushkarini is a quiet place to pause afterwards.

visit.timings: Open daily with morning and evening darshan sessions and a midday closure; festival days are busiest. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear removed before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is restricted in and around the sanctum; follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.gettingThere: Thiruninravur lies in Tiruvallur district on Chennai's western outskirts, near Avadi, and is served by Thiruninravur railway station on the Chennai Central–Arakkonam suburban line. It is reached by road from Chennai, and the nearest airport is Chennai.
